milestones.title: First written mention of Lahore
milestones.detail: The Persian geography Hudud al-'Alam names Lahore as a town with temples, markets and orchards. It is the earliest document to mention the city by name.

milestones.title: Ghaznavid conquest; Malik Ayaz made governor
milestones.detail: Mahmud of Ghazni took Lahore and appointed Malik Ayaz governor in 1021. Ayaz rebuilt and repopulated the city and raised walls and a masonry fort in 1037-1040.
milestones.source: Petersen, Dictionary of Islamic Architecture, https://archive.org/details/dictionaryofisla00andr via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lahore#Ghaznavid

milestones.title: Lahore becomes a Ghaznavid capital
milestones.detail: Lahore was made the eastern capital of the Ghaznavid Empire under Khusrau Shah, and the sole capital after Ghazni fell in 1163.
milestones.source: Glover (2008), Making Lahore Modern, University of Minnesota Press, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lahore#Ghaznavid

milestones.title: First capital of the Delhi Sultanate's Mamluk dynasty
milestones.detail: After the death of Muhammad of Ghor, Qutb ud-Din Aibak ruled from Lahore, which drew poets and scholars from across the Muslim world.

milestones.title: Mongol army sacks Lahore
milestones.detail: Lahore was sacked and ruined by a Mongol army in 1241 and held by the Mongols for some years.

milestones.title: Timur takes a much-reduced Lahore
milestones.detail: After repeated sackings in the 14th century the city had fallen into obscurity; Timur captured it in 1398 and did not loot it because it was no longer wealthy.
milestones.source: Neville (2006), Lahore: A Sentimental Journey, p. xii, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lahore#Mamluk

milestones.title: Akbar makes Lahore the Mughal capital
milestones.detail: Akbar moved his court to Lahore, refortified the ruined citadel as the brick Lahore Fort, and rebuilt and extended the city walls.

milestones.title: Shalamar Gardens laid out
milestones.detail: Shah Jahan's reign gave Lahore the Shalamar Gardens and the Wazir Khan Mosque. The pre-modern population probably peaked in this period, most of it in suburbs outside the walls.
milestones.source: UNESCO World Heritage advisory body evaluation, https://whc.unesco.org/archive/advisory_body_evaluation/171.pdf ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lahore#Shah_Jahan

milestones.title: Badshahi Mosque completed
milestones.detail: Aurangzeb's Badshahi Mosque, the largest Mughal monument in Lahore, opened in 1673, followed by the Alamgiri Gate of the fort in 1674.

milestones.title: Durrani invasions begin
milestones.detail: Ahmad Shah Durrani occupied Lahore in 1748 and returned repeatedly until 1765. By the end of the century the suburbs lay abandoned and the remaining population lived inside the walls.

milestones.title: Ranjit Singh takes Lahore
milestones.detail: Ranjit Singh captured the city in 1799 and made it the administrative capital of the Sikh Empire. By 1812 he had added a second circuit of outer walls and a moat.
milestones.source: Glover (2008), Making Lahore Modern; Latif (1892), Lahore: Its History, Architectural Remains and Antiquities, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lahore#Sikh_Empire

milestones.title: Punjab annexed by the British
milestones.detail: The East India Company, in control of Lahore since 1846, annexed the Punjab in 1849. The British laid out the Civil Station and The Mall south of the Walled City and a cantonment at Mian Mir.

milestones.title: Lahore railway station opens
milestones.detail: The fortified railway station was built just outside the Walled City shortly after the 1857 rebellion and opened in 1860.

milestones.title: Model Town founded
milestones.detail: Model Town was established as a garden-suburb, an early step in the city's spread to the south.

milestones.title: Lahore Resolution
milestones.detail: The All-India Muslim League, meeting in Lahore under Muhammad Ali Jinnah, passed the resolution demanding a separate homeland for the Muslims of India.

milestones.title: Partition: Lahore awarded to Pakistan
milestones.detail: Lahore was awarded to Pakistan on 17 August 1947 and became capital of Pakistani Punjab. Riots destroyed about 6,000 of the city's 82,000 homes, most Hindus and Sikhs left, and refugees arrived from the east.
milestones.source: Kudaisya & Yong (2004), The Aftermath of Partition in South Asia, pp. 176-177, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lahore#Partition

milestones.title: Lahore Metrobus opens
milestones.detail: The first 27 km of the bus rapid transit line, from Gajju Matta to Shahdara, opened on 11 February 2013.

milestones.title: Orange Line metro opens
milestones.detail: The Orange Line of the Lahore Metro was inaugurated on 25 October 2020.

notes: Start date: no definitive record of Lahore's founding exists. Hindu tradition attributes the city to Loh (Lava), son of Rama, and Ptolemy's 'Labokla' and an unnamed city described by Xuanzang in 630 CE have been proposed as Lahore, but none of these is secure; 982 CE is the first document that names the city, and excavations at Lahore Fort in 1959 found continuous occupation layers below a coin of 1025 CE, so the site was inhabited before the Ghaznavid conquest. Population: only five scholarly estimates exist before the British censuses and all are Chandler's. Nothing is recorded between 1100 and 1590 or between 1650 and 1855, so the medieval sackings (1241, 1329) and the timing of the 18th-century collapse are not resolved by the series. The Reba et al. digitisation of Chandler also lists 34,000 for 1600, 84,000 for 1631 and 54,000 for 1700/1707; these sit between 300,000 (1590), 500,000 (1622) and 360,000 (1650) and look like transcription artefacts or partial counts, so they are left out rather than shown as a real collapse. Chandler's Mughal-era figures include the extramural suburbs. Census figures 1881-1941 are for the town of Lahore (municipality plus cantonment) as tabulated from the census reports on Wikipedia; City Population gives lower municipality-only figures for some years (for example 138,878 in 1881 and 400,075 in 1931). Landmarks: mosque and tomb heights are minaret heights. Heights could not be sourced for the Lahore Fort walls, Lahore Cathedral, Sacred Heart Cathedral, Chauburji, Data Darbar, the railway station or Gaddafi Stadium, so they are omitted. CTBUH lists only one Lahore building (Software Technology Park); the newer 150 m-class towers listed on Wikipedia have no CTBUH entry or cited height and are omitted.
